open-question.question: Where, and at what length, does the README explain the name Gurita? The naming draft holds that the name says nothing to most English speakers and that its meaning, Indonesian for octopus with the plugin as the arms that each carry a mission out on their own, should be one sentence away on the landing page. The README today explains no name: its "Why Cairn?" section is about handing long-running work to an agent, not about the word.
open-question.alternative: The root README carries one sentence on the name in the block directly under the title, beside the tagline and the pitch and above the diagram: Gurita is Indonesian for octopus, and the plugin is the arms, each carrying a mission out on its own. Nothing else in the README explains the name, the "Why" section stays about the handoff, and the host READMEs carry no explanation. It does exactly what the naming draft asks, the meaning one sentence away at the first point of contact, and the sentence doubles as a description of what the plugin does, so it costs the pitch little. It adds a third line to the densest part of the page, between title and diagram, and how it reads there depends on whether the tagline above it stays, which the README tagline question owns; a second image line next to an unchanged stone tagline would clash.

The root README glosses the name inside its opening pitch with a bare translation, a parenthetical such as "Gurita (Indonesian for octopus) brings all the important questions up…", and nothing more: no image of the arms, no section of its own, the "Why" section left about the handoff, and the three host READMEs unchanged beyond the plain rename. The cheapest possible answer to the draft's "one sentence away": the word is explained at the first place a reader meets it, with no added line on a landing page whose top is already badges, a traffic table, the title, the tagline, the pitch, and a diagram. It translates the word but drops the reason the name was chosen, the arms that each carry a mission out on their own, so the name reads as an arbitrary animal; and a "Why Gurita?" heading further down, if the section keeps that title, promises a name explanation it does not give.

The root README's "Why Cairn?" section is retitled "Why Gurita?" and opens with one sentence on the name (Indonesian for octopus, the plugin as the arms that each carry a mission out on their own), its existing paragraphs on handing long-running work to an agent following unchanged. The top of the page and the host READMEs carry no explanation. It makes the heading mean what it says, a reader asking "why this name?" finds the answer under the question, and it leads straight into the section's existing argument, since independent arms is the handoff that section describes; the top of the page stays as it is. The section sits below installation, so a reader who stops at the pitch or goes straight to the install commands never meets the meaning, which is further than the draft's "one sentence away"; and it mixes a note on the word into a section about a problem and its approach.

The root README gains a short section of its own on the name, such as "## The name", placed below the "Why" section or near the foot of the page: a paragraph saying Gurita is Indonesian and Malay for octopus, how it is pronounced (gu-RI-ta), and why the image fits, an octopus's arms each sensing and acting on their own while the head sets the goal, as a mission resolves its own questions and runs beside others. The pitch block and the "Why" section carry no explanation, and the host READMEs none. It gives the name the room to land as a design statement, carrying the pronunciation and the arms-and-head image the draft records, without touching the pitch or the handoff argument. The longest explanation stands furthest from the first mention, so the reader who most needs the gloss reaches it last or never; and a paragraph on the image is prose that ages with the design it describes and leans on the orchestrator's head that ideas/kepala.md has not yet made real.

The root README carries both: one sentence on the name in the pitch block under the title (Indonesian for octopus, the plugin as the arms that each carry a mission out), and a short paragraph further down, in its own section or opening the retitled "Why Gurita?" section, adding the pronunciation and why the image fits. The host READMEs carry no explanation. The skimming reader gets the meaning at once and the curious one the reasoning, each at the depth they want, which is the fullest answer to both "one sentence away" and the empty name explanation the README has today. The name is explained twice on one page, the paragraph partly restating the sentence, and it adds the most prose of any option to a README that is otherwise about what the plugin does; the pitch-block line also depends on the tagline's fate, which the README tagline question owns.

One sentence on the name, Indonesian for octopus with the plugin as the arms that each carry a mission out on their own, stands in the pitch block under the title of the root README and of each of the three host README templates under scripts/hosts/, rendered into every hosts/ tree and published to each distribution repository; no longer explanation anywhere. Claude Code users are pointed at the distribution repository as the recommended source, so many first meet the name on a host README rather than the root one; this puts the meaning one sentence away on every landing page a reader can arrive at. The sentence is written four times in four files that can drift apart, and the host READMEs are deliberately short distribution notes; it widens the change beyond the one README the question names, and how the host READMEs open also depends on what they say of the former name, which the former-name question owns.

No README explains the name: the root README and the host READMEs say Gurita wherever they said Cairn, the "Why" section stays about the handoff under a heading that does not ask about the word, and the meaning stays recorded only in the naming draft, ideas/gurita.md, as Cairn's meaning was never stated on the landing page. It keeps the README entirely about what the plugin does and how to install it, adds nothing to maintain, and matches how the page treated the old name, which explained no word either. It goes against the naming draft's stated intent, and the rename is exactly when readers who knew the plugin as Cairn arrive asking what the new word is; a name that says nothing to most English speakers, with no gloss anywhere a user looks, reads as arbitrary and is harder to remember and spell.

open-question.question: What exactly does the 2.0.0 CHANGELOG entry say? By decision the mission fixes the entry's wording before the release task and records it as a decision, and the release applies it verbatim at its one pause. The frame is settled: sections and bullets at ### under the entry heading, one section headed exactly "### Rename Cairn to Gurita", two upgrade facts in a sentence or two each with no commands (the plugin is installed again under its new name with no cairn: alias, and live milestones are finished under the last Cairn release first), links into the documentation, and the closing Full Changelog link. The text itself is not: which sections stand beside that one, what the bullets announce, and how much the entry says of the path-addressed redesign and the milestone-to-mission rename the release also carries, which the naming draft leaves to the documentation instead of itemising them in the notes.

Are the documentation links in the 2.0.0 CHANGELOG entry pinned to the release tag or to the default branch? The entry links the README's install sections and the upgrade paragraph of docs/workflow.md for the per-host commands and the full upgrade rule, and the recorded decision names both forms without choosing one. The entry is published verbatim on four release pages and is never revised afterwards; a link to the tag keeps showing the documentation as released, while a link to the default branch follows later edits and breaks when a file or heading it names moves.

What does the documentation tell a user who holds an installed Cairn copy to do with it on each host? By decision the release notes carry no commands and point to the README's install sections and the upgrade paragraph of docs/workflow.md, and the root README links to where the upgrade steps are documented. Today the install sections hold only fresh-install commands, and the upgrade paragraph covers only finishing live milestones and re-running the bootstrap. Nothing says whether the old copy is removed, or how: the cairn marketplace and the cairn@cairn plugin in Claude Code and Codex, and the directory ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn, which Antigravity would load beside the new one. The README already carries one older note of this kind, telling an Antigravity user to delete a project-level .agents/plugins/cairn copy, whose path is an old-name literal a plain substitution would change.

When does the tracked .claude/settings.json stop enabling cairn@cairn and enable gurita@gurita instead? That entry is this checkout's one recorded install of the plugin, at project scope, and by decision a copy frozen under the name cairn runs every task of this mission and its finish. A task that rewrites the entry takes the frozen copy away from every session started after it, the release task's and the finish's included; leaving the entry as it is leaves an old-name identifier that the closing whole-tree search finds, that no decision keeps, and that the 2.0.0 tag records.

What do the root README's adoption table and the three host READMEs show for the distribution repositories' traffic badges at the release? Each reads its badges by raw URLs holding the repository name, from that repository's traffic-data branch. By decision the three uHappyLogic/gurita-<host> repositories are created fresh, and a fresh repository has no traffic-data branch until its traffic-badges workflow first runs after the first publish, so URLs rewritten to the new names show broken badges in the released README and on each new repository's landing page until then. The release procedure's own instructions for a new distribution repository add its table row only after that first run, in a commit of its own.

How are the idea drafts that describe this rename as still to come treated once it is carried out? ideas/gurita.md lays the rename out as a plan: a table of sites headed Today and After, a section on carrying it out, and three open questions it leaves to this mission. ideas/kepala.md and ideas/vscode_extension.md say they wait on the rename, and the second cites this mission's directory, which finish removes. The milestone-to-mission rename revised the naming draft to record its half as carried out and marked the questions it answered. So far only one sentence of the naming draft, on the name lookup, is covered by a decision, and the draft necessarily names Cairn, so whatever stays in it is old-name text the closing whole-tree search has to account for.

How does the closing whole-tree search account for this mission's own directory, mission_rename-cairn-to-gurita/? Its path and its three files hold the old name, the file-path half of the search matches it, and it stands until finish removes it, which by decision happens after the release, so the 2.0.0 tag records it. The completeness decision requires every hit that stays to be listed with its file, its count, and the decision that keeps it, and no decision names this directory.

Who points the cairn directory marketplace at the frozen copy before the first rename task, and is that step in the task list? The decision on the copy that runs the mission says the marketplace is pointed at the hosts/claude of a separate checkout or worktree held at the commit just before the first rename task, without saying whether a task does it or the maintainer does it by hand before the run starts. The change is made in Claude Code's own configuration outside the repository, no commit records it, and whether a session already running picks it up was never tested; the other machine-level steps, installing the renamed copies and the GitHub-side changes, are the maintainer's by decision.

Which conflicting decision stands: "Host suite timing" or "Hands-on check blocks"? "Host suite timing" orders the one task that runs the host suite after the last task that changes any host's trigger set, and counts each host's definition directory under scripts/hosts/ in that set. "Hands-on check blocks" has each host's settings.toml, a file in that directory, edited from a host suite run against the renamed installed copy: a dated "Re-checked" sentence naming the run, and the Install, Dispatch, and path bullets rewritten from it. That edit can only follow a suite run, so it changes every host's trigger set at or after the task the first entry places after the last such change.

Which conflicting decision stands: "Installed copies for suite" or "Plugin copy running mission"? "Installed copies for suite" has the maintainer bring each host's installed copy to the renamed build before the suite runs, with the host's documented install as CONTRIBUTING.md states it, which for Claude Code is a directory marketplace on this checkout with the plugin installed at a scope outside any project, so from then on every session on the machine loads the renamed plugin from the working tree's hosts/claude. "Plugin copy running mission" says nothing loads from the working tree's hosts/ during the mission, and that the marketplace is added from the working tree's hosts/claude under the name gurita only after the finish. The suite runs before the release, and the release before the finish.
